newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Punjab province to levy farm income tax.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Punjab province to levy farm income tax.

text.p: The caretaker government of Pakistan's Punjab province decided on Wednesday to levy a long-resisted agricultural income tax, officials said.
The provincial government expects to raise 1.2 billion rupees ($30 million) a year from the tax in populous Punjab, where Pakistan's richest farmland is located.
Elected Punjab governments have previously blocked all attempts to impose agricultural income tax.

Officials said the provincial cabinet had approved the tax, to be assessed on the basis of landholding, and the Punjab governor would sign an ordinance to implement it. Ordinances must be approved by the provincial assembly within three months.

The Punjab caretaker government was formed after the removal of the provincial assembly last month. All provincial assemblies were dismissed after President Farooq Leghari dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
The tax will be levied on Punjab farmers with at least 12.5 acres (five hectares) of irrigated or 25 acres of rain-fed land.

Farmers with more than 12.5 acres but less than 25 acres of irrigated land will pay 100 rupees per acre. Those with more than 25 but less than 50 acres will pay 125 rupees per acre. Those with 50 acres and above will pay 150 rupees per acre.
In rain-fed areas the tax rate for holdings of 25 to 50 acres will be 62.5 rupees per acre. Holdings of more than 50 acres will be taxed at 75 rupees per acre.
Under the law, farmers will be allowed to submit an income tax return on a self-assessed basis if they believe their income is lower than the government estimate.

Farmers with less than 12.5 acres, accounting for 79 percent of the total cultivated area of the province, are tax-exempt. In Sindh province the tax threshold was set at eight acres and in North West Frontier Province at five acres.
Pakistan's wealthy landowners have long escaped the tax net in a country which has an estimated 1.2 million tax-payers among a population of 131 million.
